title: Position sizing for monthly gold-futures accumulation — when a backtest answers with the top of the tested range
strategy: none — 1OZ futures accumulation and position sizing
question: Four monthly buys of gold futures from September, held to the following March: which leverage survives, and does the historical answer or the arithmetic one govern?
hypothesis: The backtest will clear every tested size because the September window has never contained a large drawdown, and that is a fact about eighteen samples rather than about the calendar.

findings.title: The question as usually asked answers with the top of the tested range
findings.detail: "The largest size with a zero margin-call rate" cannot be answered by eighteen September-to-March cycles whose worst trough against average cost is -14.18%, because the tightest margin trigger among the sizes tested is -18.96%. Every size clears, so the answer is whatever the range topped out at — 4.34x leverage here, and it would have been higher had higher been tested. That is a fact about eighteen draws, not about the calendar.

findings.title: The arithmetic gives a different answer and it is the one that governs
findings.detail: Gold fell 29.44% between January and June 2026, the largest fall in the daily record. Margin call arrives at -28.17% at 3.1x leverage and -22.8% at 3.72x, so only 2.48x and below survive a repeat: its trigger is -36.24%. The fall happened outside the September build window, which is exactly why the backtest does not see it and cannot be used to rule it out.

findings.title: Surviving margin and surviving the holder are different sizes
findings.detail: Two drawdowns are reported and they are not the same quantity. Trough against average cost is what margin tests, because maintenance compares equity to a requirement and equity is price minus cost. Peak-to-trough on the equity curve is larger and is what the position felt like: 37.09% at 2.48x leverage, and the worst case is a cycle that finished 20% up. It built near 3,900, rode gold to 5,597 in January and exited at 4,683, giving back a quarter of the account from its high on the way.

findings.title: The seasonal premise is half backwards, and unresolvable in either direction
findings.detail: A December-to-March seasonal strength is often asserted. December and January are the strong pair; February and March are the two weakest months of the year, so holding to end-March captures January and then sits through both. But no month separates: 47 observations against a resolvable gap of about 21 percentage points, with the strongest month 11.7 points clear of the rest. The claim is neither supported nor refuted, and exit timing is reported as a parameter with its bound rather than as a recommendation.

findings.title: Roll cost is excluded, and it is the largest omission
findings.detail: Carry on a 4,650 contract at prevailing rates puts a two-month roll near $36 an ounce while the front-month basis measurable here is $1 to $3 — and that basis is not the calendar spread, so it cannot settle the question. Two to three rolls sit between September and March. Against a mean cycle return of 6.2% of capital the difference between a token roll cost and a carry-implied one is most of the profit, so every figure here is optimistic and the leverage ceiling is an upper bound.

card_summary: Four monthly buys of gold futures held to March. The backtest clears every size tested because eighteen September cycles never met a large drawdown; the arithmetic stops well short.
